checks.claim: Key: with one wire from the battery's top to the bulb's base and nothing else touching, the bulb stays dark because there is no path back to the battery (no complete loop)
checks.note: A break anywhere in the loop de-energizes the lamp; the NSTA probe confirms a bulb needs current in at one contact and out at the other, on round to the battery. Wikipedia: 'An electrical circuit is a network consisting of a closed loop, giving a return path for the current.'

checks.claim: Wrong choice: one wire is too thin to carry enough electricity
checks.note: Wrong: the same single wire lights the bulb when the base tip also touches the other terminal, so thickness is not the cause.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: the electricity needs a switch to start it flowing
checks.note: Wrong: a switch only opens or closes the loop; a closed loop with no switch carries current.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: the electricity is used up inside the wire
checks.note: Wrong, and a named misconception: current is not used up; with no loop none flows at all.

checks.claim: Context: if the tip of the bulb's base also touches the battery's other end, one wire can light it
checks.note: NSTA: wire from the flat end to the side of the base, then touch the tip of the base to the bumpy end and the bulb lights.

checks.claim: Key: switching on brings metal contacts together and closes the circuit
checks.note: Grokipedia: contacts are metallic; 'When a pair of contacts is touching current can flow between them'; closed state = on position, open state = off position.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: metal touched metal and opened the circuit
checks.note: Wrong: touching contacts make the switch closed, not open.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: plastic touched plastic and closed / opened the circuit
checks.note: Wrong: a switch's plastic is its insulating body, not the contacts; ordinary plastic does not conduct.

checks.claim: Context: 'open' and 'closed' run opposite to a door's meanings; plastic could never carry it across
checks.note: All About Circuits: 'in the context of doors they hold opposite meanings'. Optional polish: 'plastic could never carry it across' is absolute and conductive plastics exist (Nobel Prize 2000), so 'the switch's plastic could not carry it across' is safer; as written it reads as the switch's own plastic and is true.

checks.claim: Key: in a single loop, a switch after the bulb still turns it off, because a gap anywhere stops the current all the way round
checks.note: All About Circuits: 'any break in the circuit at any location causes the lamp to immediately de-energize.' Geniebook: 'It doesn't matter where that gap is in a simple series circuit.'

checks.claim: Wrong choice: it stays lit, for the gap lies beyond it
checks.note: Wrong; a named misconception (a switch after the bulb cannot turn it off).

checks.claim: Wrong choice: it dims, for the switch lets less through
checks.note: Wrong for an on/off switch: separated contacts let no current flow (a dimmer is a different device, and the stem says turned off).

checks.claim: Wrong choice: it glows on until the wire runs empty
checks.note: Wrong: the wire stores no supply of electricity; the current stops at once round the loop (a filament's afterglow lasts a fraction of a second, from heat, not from stored electricity).

checks.claim: Key: house and lamp-cord wiring is copper, chosen for conductivity and for bending without cracking
checks.note: Grokipedia: copper is 'the predominant choice for building and appliance wiring'; its ductility allows bending and pulling through conduit without cracking. Grokipedia Electrical_wiring: copper is the usual choice for home branch circuits (aluminium mainly for service entrances and large feeders, not the wires in walls or lamp cords).

checks.claim: Wrong choice: Iron
checks.note: Wrong: iron 10.3 MS/m against copper 58-59.6 MS/m; not used for house wiring.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: Silver (would fit the stem's reasons, conducts even better and is ductile)
checks.note: Wrong as 'which metal is it': the stem asks which metal the wires are actually made of, and house wires are not silver (far too costly). Not defensible.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: Gold
checks.note: Wrong: gold (41.1 MS/m) conducts less well than copper and is used as plating and thin bonding wires, not house wiring.

checks.claim: Context: copper conducts better than every metal except silver
checks.note: Table at 20 C: silver 63.0, copper 58.0 (annealed; 59.6 pure), gold 41.1, aluminium 35.5, iron 10.3 (x10^6 S/m).

checks.claim: Context: silver costs fifty to a hundred times as much as copper
checks.note: Out of date. Silver was $45.26 per troy ounce on 19 Nov 2026 (about $1,455 a kg); LME copper was about $12,500-13,200 a tonne mid-November 2026 (https://news.metal.com/newscontent/HPSJFB5W7OIYMM4YPU4ZEOJU7MTVWGRUBNTCQ2A-lme-copper-hits-four-month-low-as-ai-selloff-and-china-weakness-weigh), so silver now costs about 110-115 times as much by weight (more by volume, as silver is denser). Grokipedia's '50-100 times' is a historical range. Fix: 'silver costs about a hundred times as much' or, to survive market swings, 'silver costs many times as much'.

checks.claim: Context: gold conducts less well than copper, iron about a sixth as well
checks.note: Iron 10.3 / copper 58-59.6 = 0.17-0.18, about a sixth.

checks.claim: Context: tall power lines between towers are mostly aluminium, which is lighter
checks.note: Grokipedia: aluminium conductor steel-reinforced (ACSR) cables predominate for overhead lines; aluminium is lighter, reducing tower loading and cost.

checks.claim: Key: the plastic coat keeps electricity from reaching a hand
checks.note: Oak Year 6: 'To help keep us safe from electrical shocks, wires are covered by electrical insulators made from plastic or rubber.' (Insulation also prevents short circuits between the cord's wires, per Grokipedia Electrical_wiring, but that is not among the choices, so the key stands.)

checks.claim: Wrong choice: it helps electricity flow along the wire faster
checks.note: Wrong: an insulator resists current; it does not speed it.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: it slows electricity down to a safe speed
checks.note: Wrong: safety comes from blocking the current from the body, not from any 'safe speed'. (Insulation does slightly slow high-frequency signals in cables, a velocity-factor effect irrelevant to a lamp cord and to safety, so not defensible.)

checks.claim: Wrong choice: it stores some electricity for the lamp
checks.note: Wrong: insulation prevents leakage and shorts; it is no store for the lamp.

checks.claim: Context: plastic is an insulator, keeps current in the wire; a cracked cord with bare wire showing is dangerous
checks.note: Oak Year 4: an insulator does not let electricity pass easily; plastic is the first example. 'It does not change how the current flows in the wire, and it stores none' is a fair child-level statement for a mains lamp cord (a cord's tiny capacitance is negligible).

checks.claim: Key: insulators hold the lines away from the steel towers
checks.note: Grokipedia: insulators are used for 'electrically isolating conductors from supporting structures'. Illinois Physics Van: the insulation is at the ceramic insulators that hold the bare wires away from poles and towers (https://van.physics.illinois.edu/ask/listing/1341).

checks.claim: Wrong choice: steel does not let electricity pass through it
checks.note: Wrong: carbon steel conducts (about 7 x 10^6 S/m); ACSR lines even carry steel cores.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: the electricity moves too fast to turn aside
checks.note: Wrong: current follows any conducting path offered; speed does not keep it in the line.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: rubber pads under the towers block it
checks.note: Wrong: towers and poles are grounded (MIT: the pole is 'buried deep in the ground'); the insulation is up at the cross-arms, not under the tower.

checks.claim: Context: lines are bare metal and hang from insulators of glass, porcelain or tough plastic
checks.note: IPM: the wires are 'actually not insulated at all'. Grokipedia names porcelain, glass and polymer/composite insulators. Optional polish: a composite insulator is a fibreglass-reinforced resin rod in a silicone-rubber (or EPDM) housing (https://eepower.com/technical-articles/introduction-to-transmission-line-insulator-design/); 'tough plastic' is a fair child word for the fibreglass-reinforced plastic rod, but 'glass, porcelain, or fibreglass sheathed in rubber' is more exact. Not an error.

checks.claim: Context: steel is a metal and conducts electricity well
checks.note: True at this grade: steel is a conductor (about an eighth of copper's conductivity, millions of times better than any insulator).

checks.claim: Key: tap water, with dissolved minerals, lets electricity pass
checks.note: USGS: 'Even a small amount of ions in a water solution makes it able to conduct electricity'; tap water contains 'significant amounts of dissolved substances, minerals, and chemicals'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: it blocks electricity, as rubber does
checks.note: Wrong for tap water (true only of pure water, which the stem excludes by naming the minerals). Wikipedia: drinking water 5 x 10^-4 to 5 x 10^-2 S/m, deionised 4.2 x 10^-5 S/m.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: soaks up and holds electricity; pulls it in like a magnet
checks.note: Wrong: water with dissolved minerals conducts; it neither stores nor attracts electricity.

checks.claim: Context: perfectly pure water barely lets any through
checks.note: Handled honestly: USGS calls pure water 'an excellent insulator'; 'barely lets any through' is accurate (ultrapure water still conducts a trace from self-ionization).

checks.claim: Context: 'So nothing with a plug is used beside a bath, a sink or a pool'
checks.note: As a description this is false for sinks: the US National Electrical Code (210.52(D)) requires at least one outlet within 3 ft of every bathroom basin (GFCI-protected), and hair dryers and shavers are used there daily. It is true as a safety rule (BC Hydro: 'Never use anything with a cord or plug around water'). Fix: frame it as the rule, e.g. 'So the safety rule is to keep anything with a plug away from a bath or a pool, and to dry wet hands before touching a switch', or drop 'a sink'.

checks.claim: Key: the crow is not hurt because it is not part of a complete loop
checks.note: The standard explanation: Illinois Physics Van, 'you need a complete circuit to flow current through the bird to cause it damage'; Edison: a bird on a wire does not complete a circuit (https://energized.edison.com/stories/why-can-birds-sit-safely-on-power-lines). The exact physics (MIT: 'its two feet are at the same electrical potential') is that no voltage drives current through the bird; the key is the accepted child-level form.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: the line is wrapped in a coat of plastic
checks.note: Wrong: tower lines are bare ('actually not insulated at all'; Illinois: insulation would overheat under load).

checks.claim: Wrong choice: a bird's body does not let electricity through
checks.note: Wrong: birds that touch two wires, or a wire and a pole, are electrocuted, so their bodies conduct. No choice raises the feet or the bird's size, so none is partly true.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: the line's electricity is too weak to hurt it
checks.note: Wrong: a bird's wings brushing two phases is 'rather deadly for them'.

checks.claim: Context: 'a bird touching just one line gives it no path through its body'
checks.note: Overstated: the bird's body does form a side path beside the short stretch of wire between its feet; Illinois says a bird on one wire carries 'only a tiny current, because most of it stays in the wire'. What it lacks is a path to the ground or to another wire. Fix: 'a bird touching just one line gives the electricity no path through its body to the ground or to another wire, so almost none flows through it.'

checks.claim: Context: a bird touching two lines, or a line and a tower, completes a loop and can be killed; lines are bare and carry deadly electricity
checks.note: MIT: dangerous for a bird to sit on the pole and touch a wire; Edison: touching two wires 'would create a circuit'.

checks.claim: Key: the whole unbroken path is a circuit
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'An electrical circuit is a network consisting of a closed loop, giving a return path for the current.'

checks.claim: Wrong choice: a current
checks.note: Wrong: current is 'the flow of electric charge through a conducting medium', not the path.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: a conductor
checks.note: Wrong: a conductor is a material that lets electricity pass easily (in trade use also a single wire), never the whole loop.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: a cable; context: a cable is a bundle of wires in one coat, one part of a circuit
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'an assembly of one or more insulated electrical conductors under a common or integral jacket'.

unit_notes: Checked 2026-11-25. One error: the silver/copper price ratio (50-100x) is out of date; at November 2026 prices it is about 110-115x by weight. Two uncertain wording points in contexts: the bath question's 'nothing with a plug is used beside a sink' (US code requires outlets by basins; frame it as a safety rule), and the bird question's 'no path through its body' (add 'to the ground or to another wire'). The four points the lead flagged hold: bird key is the standard complete-circuit answer and no wrong choice is partly true; tap water conducts via dissolved ions and pure water is handled honestly; tower insulators are glass, porcelain or composite; a switch after the bulb works in a simple loop.
